title: Dispersal Limitations Restrict Predicted Climate‐Driven Biodiversity Dynamics Across North America
content:
ABSTRACT

Aim

Species may not fully track shifting climatic conditions when dispersal is limited, yet how species-specific dispersal constraints scale up to shape biodiversity redistribution across taxa remains unclear. We evaluated how dispersal limitation modifies projected biodiversity dynamics under climate change.

Location

North America.

Time Period

Contemporary to late 21st century.

Major Taxa Studied

Terrestrial vertebrates.

Methods

We developed species distribution models for 256 terrestrial vertebrate species spanning dispersal rates from 0 to ~100 km/year. We compared climate-driven projections based on climatic suitability with projections incorporating species-specific dispersal constraints. We further assessed how dispersal capacity influences habitat accessibility and projected overlap with major land-cover categories and protected areas.

Results

Dispersal limitation substantially altered the magnitude and spatial structure of projected biodiversity change. Climate-driven projections predicted increasing species richness and poleward range expansion, whereas dispersal-limited projections suppressed leading-edge expansion, amplified range contraction and generated extensive climatically suitable but inaccessible habitat. These effects intensified under stronger climate forcing and were most pronounced at high latitudes. Species with lower dispersal capacities experienced substantially greater mismatches between climatically suitable and accessible habitat. Dispersal limitation also altered projected landscape overlap: overlap with forests, wetlands, and protected areas increased under climate-driven projections but declined when dispersal constraints were incorporated, whereas dispersal limitation attenuated projected increases or amplified projected declines in other landscape categories.

Main Conclusions

Species-specific dispersal capacity acts as a biological filter on climate tracking, and climate-driven projections may therefore overestimate species' ability to track environmental change. These species-level constraints scale up to alter continental biodiversity redistribution and its spatial correspondence with different landscape types. Incorporating dispersal processes is therefore essential for projecting future biodiversity change and informing conservation planning.
